lessons.title: Introduction to Logical Reasoning
lessons.description: Understand logical thinking, deductive reasoning, inductive reasoning and problem-solving techniques.
lessons.content:
Logical reasoning is the ability to analyze information, recognize relationships and draw valid conclusions. It is commonly tested in placement aptitude examinations.

Two important reasoning approaches are deductive and inductive reasoning.

Deductive reasoning starts with general rules and derives conclusions that must follow if the premises are true.

Example:
Premise 1: All software developers are employees.
Premise 2: Ravi is a software developer.
Conclusion: Ravi is an employee.

The conclusion follows logically from the premises.

Inductive reasoning identifies patterns and suggests likely conclusions, but these conclusions are not guaranteed.

Example: A company has hired graduates from a college for five consecutive years. It may hire graduates again next year, but that is not certain.

Common placement reasoning topics include number series, letter series, analogies, classifications, syllogisms, blood relations, directions, coding-decoding and arrangements.

A useful solving method is:
1. Read the question carefully.
2. Identify the given facts.
3. Separate facts from assumptions.
4. Look for patterns or relationships.
5. Eliminate unsupported conclusions.
6. Verify the final answer.

Important distinction: A statement may sound realistic without being logically supported. In reasoning questions, use the stated information rather than personal assumptions.

Placement tip: Accuracy is more important than guessing a pattern too quickly.

lessons.title: Number Series and Letter Series
lessons.description: Identify arithmetic, geometric, alternating and alphabetical patterns.
lessons.content:
Series questions test the ability to identify relationships between consecutive or alternating terms.

Arithmetic series:
2, 5, 8, 11, 14, ?
Each term increases by 3.
Answer = 17.

Geometric series:
3, 6, 12, 24, ?
Each term is multiplied by 2.
Answer = 48.

Square number series:
1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ?
These are consecutive perfect squares.
Answer = 36.

Increasing difference series:
2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ?
Differences are 2, 3, 4, 5.
Next difference = 6.
Answer = 22.

Alternating series:
2, 10, 4, 20, 6, 30, ?
Odd-position terms: 2, 4, 6, 8.
Even-position terms: 10, 20, 30.
Answer = 8.

Letter series use alphabet positions: A=1, B=2, ..., Z=26.

Example: A, C, F, J, O, ?
Positions are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15.
Differences are 2, 3, 4, 5.
Next difference = 6.
Position 21 = U.

For alphabet patterns, check forward shifts, backward shifts, alternating positions and repeated cycles.

Placement tip: Examine differences first, then multiplication, squares, cubes and alternating patterns.

lessons.title: Analogies and Classification
lessons.description: Recognize relationships between words, numbers and objects and identify the odd one out.
lessons.content:
Analogy questions test whether two pairs share the same relationship.

Example: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
A doctor commonly works in a hospital. A teacher commonly works in a school.
Answer = School.

Example: Bird : Fly :: Fish : ?
The relationship is a typical form of movement.
Answer = Swim.

Number analogy:
4 : 16 :: 7 : ?
The relationship is squaring the number.
4 squared = 16.
7 squared = 49.

Common analogy relationships include occupation and workplace, object and function, cause and effect, part and whole, synonym and antonym, and mathematical operations.

Classification questions ask which item does not belong to a group.

Example: Apple, Mango, Banana, Carrot.
Apple, Mango and Banana are fruits. Carrot is a vegetable.
Answer = Carrot.

Number classification:
4, 9, 16, 25, 30.
The first four are perfect squares. 30 is not.
Answer = 30.

Letter classification:
AB, CD, EF, GH, JK.
The first four pairs contain consecutive alphabet letters. JK is also consecutive, so no unique odd item is established by that rule. This illustrates why a valid classification question must have a clear distinguishing property.

Solving strategy:
1. Identify the relationship shared by most items.
2. Test whether the relationship applies consistently.
3. Eliminate options that violate the relationship.
4. Avoid choosing an answer based on an arbitrary property.

Placement tip: Prefer the simplest consistent relationship supported by the question.

lessons.title: Syllogisms and Logical Conclusions
lessons.description: Understand categorical statements, valid conclusions and Venn-diagram reasoning.
lessons.content:
Syllogisms involve drawing conclusions from statements about groups or categories.

Common statement forms:
All A are B.
Some A are B.
No A are B.
Some A are not B.

Example 1:
All programmers are professionals.
All professionals are employees.
Conclusion: All programmers are employees.
This conclusion follows.

Example 2:
All cats are animals.
Some animals are pets.
Conclusion: Some cats are pets.
This conclusion does not necessarily follow because the pet animals might not include cats.

Example 3:
No squares are circles.
All squares are shapes.
Conclusion: No squares are circles.
This follows directly from the first premise.

Venn diagrams can help visualize relationships between sets.

For All A are B, represent A as a subset of B.
For No A are B, represent the sets as disjoint.
For Some A are B, mark an overlap containing at least one member.

Important: In standard formal logic, 'All A are B' does not by itself establish that any A exists. Therefore, avoid inferring 'Some A are B' without an existence premise. Some aptitude tests use different conventions, so follow the examination's stated rules.

Common mistakes:
1. Reversing an all-statement.
2. Treating a possible conclusion as a necessary conclusion.
3. Assuming unstated relationships.
4. Confusing 'some' with 'all'.

Placement tip: A conclusion follows only when it is guaranteed by the given premises.

lessons.title: Blood Relations, Directions and Basic Arrangements
lessons.description: Solve family relationships, directional movement and simple seating-arrangement problems.
lessons.content:
Blood relation questions describe family connections and require identifying relationships between people.

Example: A is the father of B. B is the mother of C.
A is C's maternal grandfather.

Use a family tree to represent relationships clearly. Do not assume a person's gender unless the question states it or the relationship logically establishes it.

Direction sense questions involve north, south, east and west.

Example: A person walks 3 km east and then 4 km north.
The straight-line distance from the starting point is sqrt(3 squared + 4 squared) = 5 km.
The final position is northeast of the starting point.

Direction changes:
Facing north, turning right means east.
Facing east, turning right means south.
Facing south, turning right means west.
Facing west, turning right means north.

Seating arrangements test positions and ordering.

Example: Five students A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north.
A is immediately left of B.
C is immediately right of B.
D sits at the extreme left.
E sits at the extreme right.

One valid arrangement is D, A, B, C, E.

For arrangements, draw numbered positions and apply each clue systematically. Distinguish between 'immediately left' and 'somewhere to the left'.

When people face south, their left and right directions are reversed relative to a viewer looking at the arrangement from the front.

Problem-solving strategy:
1. Draw a family tree, compass or seating diagram.
2. Record confirmed relationships first.
3. Apply remaining clues.
4. Check all conditions.
5. Avoid assuming information not supplied.

Placement tip: Visual diagrams are usually more reliable than trying to remember every relationship mentally.

quizzes.question: Find the next number: 2, 4, 8, 16, ?
quizzes.explanation: Each term is multiplied by 2. The next term is 32.

quizzes.question: Find the next number: 3, 6, 9, 12, ?
quizzes.explanation: Each term increases by 3. The next term is 15.

quizzes.question: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
quizzes.explanation: A doctor commonly works in a hospital, while a teacher commonly works in a school.

quizzes.question: Find the odd one out: Apple, Mango, Banana, Carrot.
quizzes.explanation: Carrot is a vegetable, while the others are fruits.

quizzes.question: If A=1, B=2 and C=3, what is the sum of the alphabet positions of CAT?
All programmers are employees. All employees are professionals. Which conclusion follows?
quizzes.explanation: The subset relationship is Programmers within Employees within Professionals.

quizzes.question: A person walks 3 km east and 4 km north. What is the shortest distance from the starting point?
quizzes.explanation: Using the Pythagorean theorem, distance = sqrt(3² + 4²) = 5 km.

quizzes.question: A is the father of B. B is the mother of C. How is A related to C?
quizzes.explanation: A is the father of C's mother, making A the maternal grandfather.

quizzes.question: Find the next letter: A, C, F, J, O, ?
quizzes.explanation: Alphabet positions are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. The next increment is 6, giving position 21, U.

quizzes.question: Statements: All cats are animals. Some animals are pets. Which conclusion must follow?
options: None of these conclusions necessarily follows
quizzes.explanation: The premises do not establish whether cats overlap with the animals that are pets.

exercises.title: Number Series Pattern Challenge
exercises.instructions: Find the next two terms in each series and explain the pattern: (a) 5, 10, 15, 20; (b) 2, 6, 18, 54; (c) 1, 4, 9, 16.

exercises.title: Analogy and Odd-One-Out Practice
exercises.instructions: Solve these questions with explanations: (a) Book : Reading :: Pen : ? (b) 5 : 25 :: 8 : ? (c) Find the odd one out: 4, 9, 16, 25, 35.

exercises.title: Syllogism Conclusion Analysis
exercises.description: Evaluate which conclusions necessarily follow from given premises.
exercises.instructions: Statements: All engineers are graduates. All graduates are educated people. Determine whether each conclusion follows: (1) All engineers are educated people. (2) All educated people are engineers. (3) Some educated people are not graduates. Explain your reasoning without assuming extra facts.

exercises.title: Blood Relations and Direction Sense
exercises.description: Solve family relationships and movement-based reasoning problems.
exercises.instructions: Part A: P is the mother of Q. Q is the father of R. Determine P's relationship to R. Part B: A person walks 6 km north, 8 km east and 6 km south. Find the final direction and shortest distance from the starting point.

exercises.title: Logical Arrangement Challenge
exercises.description: Solve a seating arrangement using multiple constraints.
exercises.instructions: Five students A, B, C, D and E sit in a straight row facing north. D sits at the extreme left. E sits at the extreme right. B sits in the middle. A sits immediately left of B, and C sits immediately right of B. Determine the complete seating order and verify every clue.
